rationale: Cervical cancer screening: Pap 3-yearly ages 21-29, co-test 5-yearly ages 30-65. Stop at 65 with adequate prior negative screens.

question: A 25-year-old at 20 weeks presents with a 2 cm firm breast mass that she noticed 2 weeks ago. Ultrasound shows a solid, irregular mass. What is the most appropriate diagnostic approach?

options.rationale: Any suspicious breast mass in pregnancy requires definitive diagnosis without delay. Breast cancer aggressiveness is similar in pregnancy.
MRI with contrast has limited safety data in pregnancy and is not first-line for evaluating breast masses. Ultrasound + biopsy is preferred.
Mammogram can be performed safely in pregnancy with abdominal shielding but is adjunctive to ultrasound and biopsy, not a replacement.
A solid, irregular breast mass in pregnancy requires tissue diagnosis. Core needle biopsy is safe during pregnancy and is the gold standard for diagnosis.

rationale: Suspicious breast mass in pregnancy: ultrasound + core needle biopsy. Mammogram with shielding is safe. Cancer treatment depends on gestational age.

question: A 26-year-old primigravida at 34 weeks presents with BP 160/105, proteinuria 3+, and severe headache. Platelets 90, ALT 120, Cr 1.2. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: MgSO4 is for seizure prophylaxis, not treatment of underlying disease. Delivery remains the definitive management.

options.text: Deliver after corticosteroid course if stable
options.rationale: Severe preeclampsia at ≥34 weeks requires delivery. A short course of steroids for fetal lung maturity can be given if maternal and fetal status permit delay.
Severe preeclampsia requires inpatient management with IV antihypertensives and monitoring. Outpatient care is for mild disease only.
Severe preeclampsia with end-organ damage precludes expectant management. Delaying delivery risks eclampsia, hepatic rupture, and maternal death.

rationale: Severe preeclampsia ≥34 weeks: deliver after steroids. MgSO4 for seizure prophylaxis. BP control with labetalol or hydralazine.

question: A 27-year-old at 32 weeks presents with painless bright red vaginal bleeding. No contractions. Fundal height appropriate. What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic step?

options.rationale: BPP assesses fetal wellbeing but does not diagnose the cause of bleeding. Placental localization is the priority.
Digital exam is contraindicated when previa is suspected due to risk of provoking catastrophic hemorrhage.

options.text: Amniocentesis to assess fetal lung maturity
options.rationale: Amniocentesis has no role in diagnosing the cause of acute third-trimester bleeding and carries procedural risk.
Painless third trimester bleeding is placenta previa until proven otherwise. Ultrasound is first-line and safe. Digital exam is contraindicated.

rationale: Painless third trimester bleeding: ultrasound to locate placenta. NO digital exam. If previa confirmed: admit, steroids, deliver at 36-37 weeks if stable.

question: A 28-year-old at 36 weeks presents with sudden severe abdominal pain and dark vaginal bleeding. Uterus is rigid and tender. FHR shows late decelerations. BP 85/50. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Abruption with non-reassuring fetal status and maternal hemodynamic instability requires emergency delivery. DIC is a life-threatening complication.
Abruption is a clinical diagnosis. Delaying delivery for imaging risks fetal demise.
Fetal distress and maternal instability mandate immediate delivery. Expectant management risks fetal death and maternal coagulopathy.
Tocolysis is contraindicated in abruption. Uterine contractions may worsen bleeding and fetal compromise.

rationale: Abruptio placentae with fetal distress and maternal shock: emergency delivery. Evaluate for DIC and prepare for massive transfusion.

question: A 29-year-old at 30 weeks presents with regular painful contractions and cervical dilation of 3 cm on exam. Membranes intact. Fetal status reassuring. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Preterm labor requires hospitalization for monitoring, tocolysis, and steroid administration. Outpatient management is not appropriate.
Tocolysis buys time for steroids to work (maximal effect at 48 hours). With 3 cm dilation, the patient may deliver before steroids take effect without tocolysis.
Preterm labor at <34 weeks with intact membranes and reassuring fetal status: tocolysis for 48 hours allows corticosteroids to enhance fetal lung maturity.
Delivery is indicated when tocolysis is contraindicated (chorioamnionitis, severe preeclampsia, non-reassuring fetal status) or labor is too advanced.

rationale: Preterm labor <34 weeks: tocolysis + steroids + GBS prophylaxis. If cervical dilation >6 cm or chorioamnionitis: deliver.

question: A 30-year-old at 36 weeks presents with fluid leaking per vagina for 2 hours. Pooling and ferning are positive on speculum exam. No contractions. Fetal status reassuring. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: There is no surgical method to reseal ruptured membranes. Induction or expectant management are the only options.
Tocolysis is contraindicated in PROM due to infection risk. Delivery is the goal when the cervix is unfavorable and membranes are ruptured at term.
PROM at ≥36 weeks: induction of labor is recommended to reduce chorioamnionitis risk. GBS prophylaxis should be given if indicated.
PROM at ≤37 weeks is managed by induction unless very close to term. The risk of ascending infection outweighs benefits of waiting.

rationale: PROM ≥36 weeks: induction. 34-36 weeks: steroids + induction vs expectant. <34 weeks: steroids + antibiotics + expectant management with monitoring for infection.

question: A 31-year-old delivered vaginally 20 minutes ago. Fundus is boggy and uterus is at the umbilicus. Heavy bright red bleeding continues despite fundal massage. What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacologic management?

options.rationale: Carboprost (PGF2α) is second-line when oxytocin fails. Contraindicated in asthma. Effective for atony but causes nausea, vomiting, and bronchospasm.
TXA 1 g IV is adjunctive, given within 3 hours of delivery. It reduces death from bleeding by 20% but does not replace uterotonics.
Misoprostol is third-line and less effective than oxytocin. Used when IV access is limited. Causes fever and shivering.

options.text: IV oxytocin 10-40 IU in 1 L normal saline
options.rationale: Oxytocin is first-line for uterine atony. It causes sustained uterine contraction. Dose: 10-40 IU in 1 L NS, infused at 125-200 mL/hour.

rationale: PPH: uterine massage + oxytocin first-line. Escalate: ergometrine → carboprost → misoprostol → intrauterine balloon → surgical.

question: A 32-year-old at 28 weeks has a hemoglobin of 10.2 g/dL. MCV 82, ferritin 15. Which physiologic change of pregnancy most likely contributes to this finding?

options.text: Physiologic hemodilution from plasma volume expansion
options.rationale: Plasma volume increases ~50% while red cell mass increases only ~25%, causing dilutional anemia in the second and third trimesters. This is physiologic, not pathologic.
Folate deficiency causes macrocytic anemia (high MCV). This patient's MCV is normal, making folate deficiency unlikely.
Pregnancy does not cause hemolysis. A falling hemoglobin with elevated LDH and low haptoglobin would suggest pathologic hemolysis.
Fetal iron demands increase in the third trimester, but physiologic hemodilution is the primary cause of lower hemoglobin earlier. Iron studies help distinguish.

rationale: Gestational anemia is primarily dilutional. Iron, folate, and B12 should be evaluated. Supplementation is standard regardless.

question: A 33-year-old primigravida at 10 weeks presents for initial prenatal visit. She is healthy with no chronic conditions. What routine lab tests should be ordered at this visit?

options.text: Blood type/Rh, antibody screen, CBC, HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, rubella titer, urinalysis
options.rationale: Standard first-trimester labs include blood group + antibody screen, CBC, HIV, syphilis, HBsAg, rubella, and urinalysis. These establish baseline and identify risks.

options.text: OGTT for gestational diabetes at 10 weeks
options.rationale: OGTT is performed at 24-28 weeks routinely or earlier only if risk factors (prior GDM, BMI >30). Not part of initial visit labs.
Chest X-ray is not a routine prenatal lab. TB screening is indicated only for high-risk populations (exposure, symptoms, high-prevalence country).
Amniocentesis is offered at 15-20 weeks for women ≥35 or abnormal NIPT/serum screen. Not routine at 10 weeks.

rationale: First prenatal visit: comprehensive history, blood work, urinalysis, dating ultrasound. Supplements: folic acid, iron, vitamin D.

question: A 34-year-old primigravida at 40 weeks presents with contractions every 3 minutes, cervical dilation 6 cm, 100% effaced. FHR is 145 with moderate variability. What stage of labor is this patient in?

options.rationale: Active first stage: 6-10 cm dilation, regular contractions. Nulliparous women dilate ~1 cm/hour. FHR monitoring should be continuous.
Third stage is from delivery of the infant to delivery of the placenta. This patient is still in the active phase of first stage.
Latent phase: 0-6 cm, slower progress. This patient has passed the latent-to-active transition at 6 cm.
Second stage begins at complete dilation (10 cm) and ends with delivery. This patient is not yet fully dilated.

rationale: Active phase (6-10 cm) progresses at ~1 cm/hour for nulliparas. If protraction or arrest occurs, evaluate for augmentation with oxytocin.

question: A 35-year-old G1P1 had a vaginal delivery with second-degree perineal laceration repaired. She is breastfeeding. Which contraceptive method is most appropriate at this postpartum visit?

options.text: Progestin-only pill or IUD (Cu-IUD or LNG-IUS)
options.rationale: Postpartum contraception: progestin-only methods and IUDs are safe during breastfeeding. Progestin-only pills start immediately; IUDs can be placed at 4-6 weeks postpartum.
COCs are relatively contraindicated during breastfeeding in the first 3-6 weeks due to potential effects on milk production. Progestin-only methods are preferred.
Tubal ligation is permanent and requires informed consent before or after delivery. It is not the first-line recommendation for a healthy new mother.
Natural family planning has high failure rates in the postpartum period due to unpredictable return of ovulation and cycles.

rationale: Postpartum contraception: progestin-only methods are safe during breastfeeding. IUDs placed at 4-6 weeks postpartum.

question: A 36-year-old at 39 weeks in active labor has an FHR tracing showing variable decelerations dropping to 70 bpm, lasting 60 seconds, with moderate variability between contractions. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.rationale: Fetal scalp sampling is used to clarify indeterminate tracings but is not the first step. Intrauterine resuscitation should be initiated first.

options.text: Category II (indeterminate) — continue monitoring and consider intrauterine resuscitation
options.rationale: Variable decelerations with moderate variability are Category II. Interventions: maternal repositioning, oxygen, IV fluids, amnioinfusion. If worsening, consider operative delivery.
Category I requires all: baseline 110-160, moderate variability, NO decelerations. Variables make this Category II.
Category III: absent variability + recurrent late/variables, or bradycardia. This has moderate variability, making it Category II.

rationale: Category II tracing: resuscitative measures first. If repetitive severe variables with rising baseline or minimal variability → expedite delivery.

question: A 37-year-old G2P2 on postpartum day 3 after C-section presents with fever 39°C, tachycardia, and purulent discharge from the incision site. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Mastitis presents with breast tenderness, erythema, and fever. This patient's findings are abdominal wall, not breast-related.
UTI causes dysuria, frequency, and suprapubic pain. Without urinary symptoms, wound infection is more likely.
Endometritis presents with uterine tenderness, foul lochia, and fever. This patient's primary findings are at the incision, not the uterus.
Post-cesarean fever with localized wound tenderness, erythema, and purulent drainage is a surgical site infection until proven otherwise. Wound culture and broad-spectrum antibiotics are indicated.

rationale: Post-cesarean wound infection: culture, antibiotics (coverage for MRSA if risk factors), wound opening and drainage if abscess.

question: A 38-year-old primigravida at 41 weeks 5 days with reassuring fetal status and unfavorable cervix (Bishop score 4). What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Perinatal risks increase after 41 weeks. Induction at 41 weeks reduces adverse outcomes compared to expectant management until 42 weeks.
C-section is not indicated solely for post-term with favorable Bishop score. Induction with cervical ripening is appropriate.
Antenatal testing (BPP or NST) is recommended for post-term pregnancies, but induction at 41+ weeks is still recommended regardless of testing results.
Post-term pregnancy (≥41 weeks): induction reduces perinatal mortality and meconium aspiration without increasing C-section rate. Bishop score <6 may require cervical ripening.

rationale: Post-term pregnancy ≥41 weeks: induction recommended with cervical ripening if Bishop <6. Continue fetal surveillance if awaiting spontaneous labor.

question: A 39-year-old at 34 weeks with fundal height measuring 4 weeks behind dates. Ultrasound shows estimated fetal weight <10th percentile with normal amniotic fluid and normal Doppler studies. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: SGA with normal fluid and Doppler: likely constitutional or asymmetric growth restriction. Management: serial growth scans, antenatal testing. Normal Dopplers suggest low risk of hypoxia.

options.text: Intrauterine growth restriction from placental insufficiency
options.rationale: Placental insufficiency typically presents with abnormal Dopplers (elevated umbilical artery S/D ratio), oligohydramnios, and asymmetric growth.
Amniotic fluid is normal per the scenario. Oligohydramnios would need further evaluation for PROM or placental insufficiency.
Macrosomia is defined as EFW >90th percentile or >4000 g, the opposite of this scenario.

rationale: SGA with normal Dopplers and fluid: likely constitutional. IUGR with abnormal Dopplers: closer monitoring, steroids if <34 weeks, deliver for worsening.

question: A 40-year-old at 32 weeks with severe preeclampsia is advised delivery for maternal safety. She refuses C-section due to religious beliefs about surgical delivery. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.rationale: Performing surgery without consent constitutes battery. A competent adult's refusal must be respected even if providers disagree.

options.text: Counsel thoroughly, document capacity, explore alternatives, involve ethics committee if needed
options.rationale: A competent patient has the right to refuse treatment. Explore reasons, provide alternatives, document capacity assessment. Ethics committee involvement may help resolve the conflict.

options.text: Obtain a court order for forced C-section
options.rationale: Court-ordered intervention is reserved for life-threatening emergencies when the patient lacks capacity or in specific jurisdictions for fetal viability. Counseling and alternatives should be exhausted first.
Transfer is an option but does not resolve the underlying ethical conflict. Counseling and multidisciplinary involvement are more appropriate first steps.

rationale: Competent refusal of C-section: explore concerns, document capacity, involve ethics. Forced surgery is not ethically justified.

question: A 2-month-old male presents with acute watery diarrhea for 3 days, vomiting, and decreased urine output. Dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, skin tenting. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.rationale: Holding feeds in non-severe diarrhea prolongs illness. Early refeeding is recommended. Antibiotics are not indicated for acute watery diarrhea.
Antidiarrheals are contraindicated in children due to risk of ileus, toxic megacolon, and side effects.

options.text: ORS or IV fluids based on dehydration severity
options.rationale: Assess dehydration first. Mild-moderate: ORS. Severe: IV bolus. Continue breastfeeding. Zinc 20 mg daily for 14 days reduces duration and severity.
Most gastroenteritis is viral. Antibiotics are reserved for dysentery, suspected cholera, or immunocompromised patients.

rationale: Manage dehydration severity with ORS or IV. Zinc reduces duration. Continue feeding.

question: A 3-month-old female presents with fever 39.5°C and a 3-minute generalized seizure that stopped spontaneously. Now alert and playing. No prior seizures. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Meningitis should be considered if the child is ill-appearing or has nuchal rigidity. This child returned to baseline immediately.
Simple febrile seizure: age 6m-5y, generalized, <15 min, single in 24h, no postictal deficit. No workup beyond fever source identification needed.
Complex: focal, >15 min, or multiple in 24h. This seizure is generalized, brief, and single.
Epilepsy requires 2+ unprovoked seizures. Febrile seizures are provoked by fever and generally do not predict epilepsy.

rationale: Simple febrile seizure: age 6m-5y, generalized <15min. Manage fever. No EEG or imaging needed.

question: A 4-year-old male with persistent coughing fits ending with a whooping sound, post-tussive vomiting, and no fever. Not immunized. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Bronchiolitis presents with wheezing, respiratory distress, and fever in infants <12 months. Not paroxysmal cough.
Foreign body presents with sudden onset of coughing and choking in a previously well child. Not paroxysmal with whoop.
Croup presents with barking cough, stridor, and hoarseness. Not paroxysmal whooping fits.
Pertussis: paroxysmal cough with inspiratory whoop, post-tussive vomiting, afebrile. Most severe in infants. Diagnosis: PCR or culture. Treatment: macrolide antibiotic.

rationale: Pertussis: paroxysmal cough + whoop. Macrolide treatment. Prevention: DTaP vaccine.

question: A 5-year-old female presents with wheezing and respiratory distress after playing with a cat. PEFR 40% predicted. After 3 salbutamol nebulizations and oral prednisone, PEFR remains 45%. What is the next step?

options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for impending respiratory failure (silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion). Not yet indicated.
IV MgSO4 is the next step for severe asthma not responding to SABA and steroids. It reduces hospital admission rates and improves PEFR within 30 minutes.
One dose of steroids is adequate for acute exacerbation. Additional steroids take hours to work and do not provide immediate benefit.
Aminophylline is no longer recommended in pediatric acute asthma due to side effects and lack of additional benefit beyond SABA and steroids.

rationale: Severe asthma not responding to SABA+steroids: IV MgSO4. IV salbutamol for life-threatening cases.

question: A 6-month-old male presents with Hb 8.5, MCV 70, ferritin 5. Diet history: prolonged breastfeeding with no iron-rich solids. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Lead poisoning causes microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling. History of pica or environmental exposure would be present.
ACD has normal or high ferritin and low iron/TIBC. Not associated with dietary iron deficiency.
Thalassemia minor has microcytosis out of proportion to anemia, normal ferritin, and elevated HbA2 on electrophoresis.
IDA: microcytic anemia with low ferritin from inadequate dietary iron. Most common in 9-24 month olds. Treatment: oral iron 3-6 mg/kg/day plus dietary modification.

rationale: IDA in toddlers: screen with CBC and ferritin. Treat with oral iron. Prevent with iron-fortified cereals after 6 months.

question: A 7-month-old female presents with cough, wheeze, and respiratory distress for 2 days. RSV positive. O2 88%, RR 60. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Antibiotics are for secondary bacterial infection. Most bronchiolitis is viral and antibiotics are not indicated.
Bronchodilators are not routinely recommended in bronchiolitis. May trial but discontinue if no objective improvement.

options.text: Oxygen if SpO2 <90%, nasal suctioning, supportive care
options.rationale: Bronchiolitis is managed supportively. O2 for SpO2 <90%. Nasal suctioning before feeds. Most resolves in 7-10 days. No routine bronchodilators or steroids.
Steroids do not improve outcomes in viral bronchiolitis and are not recommended unless the child has concomitant asthma.

rationale: Bronchiolitis: supportive care (O2, suctioning). No bronchodilators or steroids routinely.

question: A 8-year-old male presents with fever, cough, and tachypnea for 3 days. CXR shows right lower lobe consolidation. O2 96%, no indrawing. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Non-severe CAP: oral amoxicillin 90 mg/kg/day. Hospitalize if hypoxia, indrawing, toxic appearance, or inability to tolerate oral.
Consolidation on CXR with fever suggests bacterial pneumonia requiring antibiotics.
Hospitalization is for hypoxia, significant indrawing, or toxic appearance. This patient has no severity criteria.
Macrolides are for atypical pneumonia (Mycoplasma) in school-age children. Amoxicillin is first-line for typical lobar pneumonia in younger children.

rationale: Pediatric CAP: amoxicillin first-line. Hospitalize if hypoxia, indrawing, or toxic.

question: A 9-year-old female presents with ear pain and fever for 2 days. Otoscopy shows bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane with decreased mobility. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Observation is appropriate for children ≥2 years with mild unilateral AOM. This patient has fever and ear pain suggesting moderate severity.
Augmentin is reserved for treatment failure after 48-72 hours of amoxicillin or recent antibiotic use.
Acute otitis media: antibiotics if age <2 years, bilateral, severe symptoms, or otorrhea. Amoxicillin first-line. Observation option for older children with mild symptoms.
Tubes are for recurrent AOM (≥3 in 6 months or ≥4 in 12 months) or chronic OME, not first episode.

rationale: AOM: amoxicillin first-line. Observation for mild cases in older children. Prevention: pneumococcal and influenza vaccines.

question: A 10-year-old male presents with fever, sore throat, and exudative tonsillitis. Rapid strep test positive. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Steroids are not indicated for uncomplicated GAS pharyngitis. Antibiotics alone are sufficient.
Macrolides are alternatives for penicillin-allergic patients but are not first-line due to resistance concerns.
Rapid strep test positive confirms GAS infection. Antibiotics are indicated to prevent suppurative and non-suppurative complications.

options.text: Penicillin V or amoxicillin for 10 days
options.rationale: Group A strep pharyngitis requires antibiotics to prevent rheumatic fever. Penicillin or amoxicillin for 10 days is first-line.

rationale: GAS pharyngitis: penicillin 10 days prevents rheumatic fever. Treat even if mild.

question: A 11-month-old female presents with fever for 3 days without source. Urine dipstick shows leukocyte esterase positive and nitrite positive. Urine culture grows E. coli >10^5 CFU/mL. What is the appropriate imaging after first febrile UTI?

options.rationale: Children <2 years with first febrile UTI require renal/bladder US per guidelines.
First febrile UTI in child <2 years: renal/bladder US to assess for anatomic abnormalities. VCUG if US abnormal or recurrent UTI.
VCUG is indicated after abnormal US, recurrent UTIs, or atypical/complicated UTI. Not for all first UTIs.
DMSA evaluates renal scarring after pyelonephritis. Not routine after first UTI.

rationale: First febrile UTI in <2 years: renal US. VCUG if abnormal US or recurrent.

question: A 12-year-old male presents with chronic diarrhea, bloating, and poor weight gain. Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA strongly positive. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Budesonide is for refractory celiac disease. First-line is dietary gluten elimination.
PPIs do not treat celiac disease. They might mask symptoms without addressing the underlying autoimmune response.
Celiac disease requires strict lifelong gluten-free diet. Symptoms improve within weeks. Serology normalizes over months. Monitor for nutritional deficiencies.
Secondary lactose intolerance may coexist but gluten avoidance is the primary treatment for celiac disease.

rationale: Celiac disease: gluten-free diet. Monitor growth, serology, and nutritional status.

question: A 13-year-old female presents with palpable purpura on the legs and buttocks, abdominal pain, and arthritis. Recent URTI. Platelets normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: ITP presents with petechiae and bruising with LOW platelets. This patient has normal platelets.
Kawasaki has fever >5 days, conjunctivitis, oral changes, and extremity changes. Not palpable purpura on lower extremities.
HSP: palpable purpura + abdominal pain + arthritis. Normal platelets. Usually self-limited. Steroids for severe abdominal pain or renal involvement. Monitor urine for nephritis.
Meningococcemia presents with fever, petechial/purpuric rash, and ill appearance. This child has abdominal pain and arthritis without toxic appearance.

rationale: HSP: palpable purpura + arthritis + abdominal pain. Self-limited. Steroids for severe GI or renal involvement.

question: A 14-month-old male presents with bowed legs and widened wrists. Not yet walking. Formula-fed, limited sun exposure. Alkaline phosphatase elevated, calcium low-normal, phosphorus low. X-ray shows cupping and fraying of metaphyses. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Rickets: bowed legs, widened wrists, hypocalcemia, low phosphorus, elevated ALP. X-ray: metaphyseal cupping and fraying. Treatment: vitamin D and calcium supplementation.
Blount disease is a growth disorder of the proximal tibia causing bowing. X-ray shows tibial vara without metaphyseal changes of rickets.
Renal osteodystrophy occurs in CKD with elevated creatinine and abnormal calcium/phosphate. This patient has no renal history.
Hypophosphatasia has low ALP (not elevated), along with bone deformities and fractures.

rationale: Rickets: vitamin D + calcium supplementation. Prevent with vitamin D 400 IU/day from birth.

question: A 15-year-old female presents with constipation since infancy, ribbon-like stools, and failure to thrive. Rectal exam shows empty rectum with tight anal canal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Celiac presents with diarrhea, bloating, and malabsorption, not constipation from birth.
Congenital hypothyroidism presents with poor feeding, hypotonia, and prolonged jaundice. Constipation may occur but not ribbon-like stools.
Functional constipation develops after infancy with stool-withholding behavior, palpable fecal mass, and normal rectal tone.
Hirschsprung: constipation from birth, ribbon stools, empty rectum on exam. Diagnosis: barium enema shows transition zone. Treatment: surgical resection of aganglionic segment.

rationale: Hirschsprung: constipation from birth, empty rectum. Barium enema + rectal biopsy for diagnosis. Surgical resection.

question: A 16-month-old male presents with recurrent infections including pneumonia, oral thrush, and failure to thrive. Low immunoglobulins, absent B cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: SCID presents earlier (first months) with severe infections, lymphopenia, and failure to thrive. T cells are affected.
Hyper-IgM: normal/high IgM with low IgG/IgA/IgE, opportunistic infections (PCP, Cryptosporidium).
Bruton disease: recurrent infections starting after 6 months (maternal IgG wanes), low immunoglobulins, absent B cells. Treatment: IVIG replacement.
Wiskott-Aldrich: eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets, recurrent infections, and autoimmune disease.

rationale: Bruton agammaglobulinemia: recurrent infections after 6 months, low immunoglobulins, absent B cells. IVIG therapy.

question: A 17-year-old female presents with ascending weakness starting in the legs over 3 days, areflexia, and no sensory level. Lumbar puncture shows elevated protein with normal WBC. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: GBS: ascending paralysis, areflexia, albuminocytologic dissociation (high protein, normal cells). Often post-infectious. Treatment: IVIG or plasmapheresis.
Myasthenia gravis has fluctuating weakness, ptosis, diplopia, and fatiguability. Not ascending paralysis.
Polio presents with asymmetric flaccid paralysis with fever. Nearly eradicated due to vaccination.
Transverse myelitis has a sensory level and acute onset of paraplegia with spinal cord inflammation on MRI.

rationale: GBS: ascending paralysis, areflexia, high CSF protein. IVIG or plasmapheresis. Respiratory monitoring essential.

question: A 18-year-old male presents with a first-time afebrile generalized seizure. EEG shows generalized spike-wave discharges. Neurologic exam normal. MRI normal. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: With abnormal EEG, recurrence risk is high and treatment is recommended. Observation may be appropriate if EEG is normal.

options.text: Start antiepileptic drug (valproic acid or levetiracetam)
options.rationale: First unprovoked seizure with epileptiform EEG has ~50% recurrence risk. AED therapy reduces recurrence. Valproate or levetiracetam are first-line for generalized epilepsy.
Carbamazepine is first-line for focal seizures, not generalized spike-wave epilepsy. Valproate or levetiracetam are preferred.
Benzodiazepines are for acute active seizures or status epilepticus. This patient has already stopped seizing.

rationale: First unprovoked seizure with abnormal EEG: start AED. Valproate for generalized, carbamazepine for focal.

question: A 19-year-old female with cerebral palsy (GMFCS III) presents with worsening hip pain and difficulty sitting. X-ray shows >50% femoral head subluxation. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Botox reduces spasticity and may slow subluxation progression but does not correct established subluxation >50%.

options.text: Referral to orthopedics for surgical reconstruction
options.rationale: Hip subluxation >50% in CP requires surgical reconstruction (femoral osteotomy ± pelvic osteotomy) to prevent dislocation, pain, and loss of function.
Casting is for developmental dysplasia in infants, not for spastic hip subluxation in CP.
PT maintains range of motion but cannot reverse structural subluxation. Surgical intervention is needed.

rationale: CP hip surveillance: X-ray every 6-12 months. Surgical reconstruction for subluxation >50% or dislocation.

question: A 20-year-old male presents with episodic unilateral pounding headache with nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia. Relieved by sleep. Neuro exam normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Migraine: episodic unilateral pulsating headache, nausea, photophobia/phonophobia, relieved by sleep. Treatment: ibuprofen or sumatriptan. Prevention for frequent attacks.
Pseudotumor: headache with papilledema, visual disturbances, elevated CSF pressure. Neuroimaging is normal.
Cluster: unilateral severe pain around eye with autonomic features (lacrimation, rhinorrhea). Duration 15-180 minutes.
Tension headache: bilateral band-like pressure, no nausea or photophobia. Less disabling than migraine.

rationale: Pediatric migraine: acute treatment (NSAIDs, triptans). Prevention (amitriptyline, topiramate) for frequent attacks.

question: A 20-day-old female presents with cyanosis and respiratory distress. Pulse oximetry: preductal 95%, postductal 75%. Chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly with pulmonary edema. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: TOF presents with cyanosis and hypercyanotic spells, not differential cyanosis. Echocardiogram shows VSD, overriding aorta, RV hypertrophy, pulmonary stenosis.
TAPVR presents with cyanosis and pulmonary edema. Not differential cyanosis.
Differential cyanosis (higher preductal O2) suggests coarctation. Ductus supplies descending aorta. Start PGE1 to maintain ductal patency. Surgical repair after stabilization.
TGA presents with severe cyanosis in first day, equal pre and postductal saturations. Requires balloon atrial septostomy.

rationale: Duct-dependent coarctation: start PGE1, ICU, surgical repair. Differential cyanosis is the key sign.

question: A 22-year-old male presents with fever and joint pain 3 weeks after strep throat. Cardiac exam shows a new murmur. ECG shows prolonged PR interval. ESR elevated, ASO titer elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Rheumatic fever: Jones criteria require 2 major (carditis, arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules) or 1 major + 2 minor. Treatment: aspirin, penicillin prophylaxis.
JIA presents with prolonged fever and arthritis but not carditis or ASO elevation.
Kawasaki: fever >5 days, conjunctivitis, oral changes, rash, extremity changes. Not associated with preceding strep throat.
Endocarditis presents with fever, murmur, and positive blood cultures. Not preceded by strep throat with ASO elevation.

rationale: Rheumatic fever: follows GAS pharyngitis. Jones criteria. Penicillin prophylaxis prevents recurrence and rheumatic heart disease.

question: A 23-month-old female presents with poor feeding, tachypnea, and failure to thrive. Loud holosystolic murmur at left lower sternal border. Chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascularity. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: ASD has wide fixed splitting of S2 with systolic murmur at left upper sternal border. Often asymptomatic in infancy.
TOF presents with cyanosis and right-sided aortic arch. Murmur is systolic at left upper sternal border from pulmonary stenosis.
PDA has continuous machinery murmur at left infraclavicular area. Bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure.

Large VSD presents at 4-8 weeks (when pulmonary resistance drops) with heart failure, holosystolic murmur at LLSB, and increased pulmonary vascularity. Treatment: surgical closure if failure to thrive.

rationale: Large VSD: heart failure at 4-8 weeks. Medical management first, surgical closure if failure.

question: A 24-month-old male presents with barking cough, stridor, and hoarseness for 2 days, worse at night. Mild chest wall indrawing. O2 95%. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Bacterial tracheitis presents with high fever, toxic appearance, and thick purulent secretions. Requires intubation and antibiotics.
Croup: barking cough, stridor, hoarseness. Viral (parainfluenza). Management: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg. Nebulized epinephrine for moderate-severe stridor at rest.
Epiglottitis: acute onset, high fever, drooling, tripod positioning. Now rare due to Hib vaccine.
Foreign body: sudden onset of choking and cough in a previously well child. Not barking cough worse at night.

rationale: Croup: dexamethasone first-line. Nebulized epinephrine for moderate-severe distress.

question: A 25-year-old female presents with recurrent sinopulmonary infections, pancreatic insufficiency, and failure to thrive. Sweat chloride 85 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Asthma presents with wheezing, not pancreatic insufficiency or failure to thrive. Sweat chloride is normal.

CF: autosomal recessive, defective CFTR gene. Sweat chloride >60 confirms diagnosis. Multisystem: sinopulmonary, pancreatic, hepatobiliary, and male infertility. Treatment: airway clearance, enzymes, antibiotics.
PCD presents with chronic respiratory infections and situs inversus in 50%. Sweat chloride is normal.
SCID presents with severe infections from infancy, not chronic sinopulmonary disease with pancreatic insufficiency.

rationale: CF: sweat chloride >60 confirms diagnosis. CFTR modulators (ivacaftor) for specific mutations.

question: A 26-year-old male presents with chronic wet cough, purulent sputum, and digital clubbing. CT chest shows cylindrical bronchiectasis in the right middle lobe. What is the most common underlying cause?

options.rationale: PCD causes bronchiectasis but typically affects both lower lobes and has associated rhinosinusitis and situs abnormalities.
Bronchiectasis in children results from severe lower respiratory infection (adenovirus, pertussis), CF, immunodeficiency, or aspiration. Right middle lobe syndrome is common.
ABPA presents in asthmatics or CF patients with pulmonary infiltrates and elevated IgE. Not typical isolated lobar bronchiectasis.
Alpha-1 causes panacinar emphysema and liver disease, not bronchiectasis.

rationale: Bronchiectasis in children: investigate cause (infection, CF, immunodeficiency). Chest PT and antibiotics for exacerbations.

question: A 27-year-old female presents with fever, headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness. CSF shows WBC 1500 (80% neutrophils), glucose 1.2, protein 120. Gram-positive diplococci. What is the most likely organism?

options.rationale: Listeria: gram-positive rods. More common in neonates, elderly, and immunocompromised.
Pneumococcal meningitis: gram-positive diplococci. Common in children, especially with asplenia or cochlear implants. Treatment: ceftriaxone + vancomycin until sensitivities.
Hib meningitis: gram-negative coccobacilli. Now rare due to Hib vaccine.
Meningococcal meningitis: gram-negative diplococci. Associated with petechial rash and rapid progression. Treatment: ceftriaxone.

rationale: Bacterial meningitis: CSF with high WBC, low glucose, high protein. Empiric ceftriaxone + vancomycin pending culture.

question: A 28-year-old male presents with fever, conjunctivitis, cough, coryza, and Koplik spots. A maculopapular rash appears on day 4 starting on the face and spreading downward. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Measles: prodrome (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots), then spreading maculopapular rash. Complications: pneumonia, encephalitis, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis.
Roseola (HHV-6): high fever for 3-5 days then rash appears as fever resolves. Affects infants <2 years.
Rubella: milder rash, postauricular lymphadenopathy, low-grade fever. No Koplik spots.
Scarlet fever: sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, pharyngeal erythema. Caused by GAS exotoxin.

rationale: Measles: highly contagious. Supportive care. Vitamin A reduces morbidity and mortality. Prevention: MMR vaccine.

question: A 29-year-old female presents with 3 weeks of intermittent fever, night sweats, and cough. Contact with uncle who has chronic cough. CXR shows hilar lymphadenopathy and right upper lobe infiltrate. TST positive 15 mm. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Active pulmonary TB in children: 4-drug regimen (rifampin, INH, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for 2 months, then 2 drugs (INH + rifampin) for 4 months. Directly observed therapy.
Active TB requires 4 drugs initially due to risk of resistance. Two drugs are for the continuation phase after 2 months.
INH prophylaxis is for latent TB. This patient has active disease (symptoms + CXR findings) requiring full multi-drug therapy.
Active TB requires treatment to prevent progression, complications (miliary, meningitis), and transmission.

rationale: Active TB: 2 months RIPE → 4 months RI. LTBI: INH or rifampin alone.

question: A 30-month-old male presents with fever, poor feeding, and bulging fontanelle. Blood culture grows Haemophilus influenzae type b. The mother declined vaccination. What is the most appropriate prevention for this infection?

options.rationale: Rifampin prophylaxis is for close contacts of Hib cases, not for routine infant prevention. The vaccine is the primary prevention.

options.text: Hib vaccine series starting at 2 months
options.rationale: Hib vaccine (conjugate) at 2, 4, 6, and 12-15 months prevents invasive Hib disease (meningitis, epiglottitis, pneumonia). Decline in cases >99% since vaccine introduction.
Meningococcal vaccine prevents Neisseria meningitidis, not Hib. Two different pathogens.
PCV13 prevents Streptococcus pneumoniae, not Hib.

rationale: Hib vaccine: conjugate vaccine at 2,4,6,12-15 months. Also indicated for asplenia and sickle cell disease.

question: A 31-year-old female presents with daily fever for 10 days, conjunctival injection, red cracked lips, strawberry tongue, erythema of palms and soles, and unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: SJIA: quotidian fevers, evanescent salmon-pink rash, arthritis. Does not have conjunctival injection or oral changes typical of KD.
SJS: severe mucocutaneous reaction with target lesions, blistering, and skin sloughing. Prior drug exposure.
Kawasaki: fever >5 days + 4 of 5 mucocutaneous features. IVIG 2 g/kg within 10 days reduces coronary artery aneurysms from 25% to 5%. Aspirin high-dose then low-dose.
Scarlet fever: sandpaper rash, pharyngitis, responds to antibiotics. Does not have conjunctivitis or extremity changes of KD.

rationale: KD: IVIG + aspirin within 10 days prevents coronary aneurysms. Echo follow-up at 2 weeks and 6 weeks.

question: A 32-year-old male of Saudi descent presents with recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain, fever, and arthritis. Family history of similar episodes. Responds well to colchicine. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: SLE: multisystem autoimmune disease with positive ANA. Not episodic attacks responding to colchicine.
JIA presents with chronic arthritis, not episodic febrile attacks with serositis.
FMF: autosomal recessive, common in Arab populations. Recurrent febrile episodes with serositis, arthritis, and erysipelas-like erythema. Colchicine prevents attacks and amyloidosis.
Crohn causes chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, and weight loss. Not episodic febrile attacks responding to colchicine.

rationale: FMF: common in Arabs. Colchicine prevents attacks and secondary amyloidosis. Genetic testing confirms.

question: A 33-year-old female of Arabian Gulf origin presents with fatigue and pallor. Hb 9.5, MCV 65, HbA2 4.5%. Ferritin normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Alpha-thalassemia: low or normal HbA2 with microcytosis. More common in Southeast Asian populations.
IDA has low ferritin and elevated TIBC. This patient has normal ferritin, making thalassemia more likely.
ACD has normal or elevated ferritin with microcytic index. HbA2 is normal, not elevated.
Thalassemia minor: microcytosis with elevated HbA2, normal ferritin. Common in Gulf region. Carrier screening and genetic counseling recommended for at-risk couples.

rationale: Beta-thalassemia trait: elevated HbA2. Genetic counseling. Prenatal diagnosis for at-risk couples.

question: A 34-year-old male presents with acute onset of dark urine after eating fava beans. Hb 8.0, reticulocytes elevated, peripheral smear shows bite cells and Heinz bodies. G6PD level low. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Iron is not indicated in hemolytic anemia. Exacerbates oxidative stress. Trigger avoidance is the key.

options.text: Avoidance of oxidative triggers (fava beans, sulfa drugs, naphthalene)
options.rationale: G6PD deficiency: X-linked, common in Mediterranean and Gulf populations. Acute hemolytic anemia triggered by oxidants. Management: trigger avoidance. Transfusion if severe anemia.
Splenectomy is for hereditary spherocytosis, not G6PD deficiency. Hemolysis in G6PD is self-limited once trigger removed.
Exchange transfusion is reserved for severe neonatal hyperbilirubinemia or life-threatening hemolysis. Most cases resolve with trigger removal.

rationale: G6PD deficiency: avoid oxidative triggers. Newborn screening in high-prevalence populations (Saudi Arabia, Mediterranean).

question: A 35-year-old female presents with recurrent vaso-occlusive crises, acute chest syndrome, and HbS 85% on electrophoresis. What is the most appropriate disease-modifying therapy?

options.rationale: Penicillin prophylaxis prevents pneumococcal sepsis in SCD but is not disease-modifying. It does not reduce crises or acute chest syndrome.
Hydroxyurea increases HbF levels, reducing vaso-occlusive crises, acute chest syndrome, and transfusion needs. First-line disease-modifying therapy for SCD.
BMT is curative but reserved for severe SCD with a matched sibling donor. Not first-line due to transplant-related mortality.
Chronic transfusions are for patients with stroke risk (abnormal TCD) or severe complications despite hydroxyurea. Carries iron overload risk.

rationale: SCD: newborn screening, penicillin prophylaxis, hydroxyurea. Stroke prevention with TCD screening.

question: A 36-year-old male presents with periorbital edema, frothy urine, and weight gain. Urine protein 4+, albumin 1.8, cholesterol 350. What is the most likely diagnosis and initial therapy?

options.rationale: UTI causes dysuria and fever, not generalized edema and heavy proteinuria.
Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. Prednisone induces remission in 90%. Relapses are common but respond to steroid retreatment.
Cyclophosphamide is for steroid-resistant or frequently relapsing nephrotic syndrome, not first-line.
AGN presents with hematuria, hypertension, oliguria, and mild proteinuria. Not heavy proteinuria with hypoalbuminemia.

rationale: Nephrotic syndrome: prednisone 4-6 weeks first episode. Relapses retreated. Steroid-sparing agents for frequent relapses.

question: A 37-year-old female presents with gross hematuria, hypertension, and periorbital edema 2 weeks after strep throat. C3 low, ASO elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: PSGN: immune complex-mediated GN after GAS infection. Low C3, normal C4. Self-limited in children. Manage hypertension and fluid overload. Dialysis rarely needed.
Lupus nephritis occurs in SLE with positive ANA, anti-dsDNA, low C3 and C4. Systemic symptoms are present.
IgA nephropathy presents with hematuria coinciding with URTI (same day), not 2 weeks later. C3 is normal.
HUS: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, renal failure. Preceded by diarrheal illness (E. coli O157).

rationale: PSGN: self-limited. Manage hypertension and fluid overload. Low C3 returns to normal in 6-8 weeks.

question: A 38-month-old male presents with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure after diarrhea caused by E. coli O157:H7. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: ITP has isolated thrombocytopenia without anemia or renal failure.
ATN presents with muddy brown casts and elevated FENa. Does not have thrombocytopenia or microangiopathic hemolysis.
HUS: triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, AKI. Typical HUS follows diarrheal illness (E. coli O157, Shiga toxin). Supportive care. Dialysis if needed.
TTP has neurological symptoms, fever, and low ADAMTS13 activity. More common in adults. Rare in children.

rationale: Typical HUS: supportive care, dialysis if needed. Avoid antibiotics in E. coli O157 as they increase HUS risk.

question: A 39-year-old female presents with sudden onset of choking, coughing, and respiratory distress while eating peanuts. Breath sounds decreased on the right. What is the most appropriate immediate management if the child is conscious and has mild distress?

options.rationale: Epinephrine is for croup or anaphylaxis, not for foreign body airway obstruction.

options.text: Back blows and chest thrusts (infant) or Heimlich maneuver (child >1 year)
options.rationale: Foreign body aspiration: if conscious and choking, perform age-appropriate obstruction relief. If severe distress or unconscious, start CPR and call for help.
Bronchoscopy is definitive for diagnosis and removal but should not delay first aid for acute obstruction.
CXR may show hyperinflation or atelectasis but should not delay airway clearance in acute obstruction.

rationale: Foreign body aspiration: airway clearance maneuvers first. Bronchoscopy for definitive removal.

question: A 40-year-old male presents with fever, petechiae, and lethargy 2 hours after onset. BP 70/40. Widespread petechial rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Meningococcemia: rapidly progressive fever, petechial/purpuric rash, hypotension. Medical emergency: IV ceftriaxone, fluid resuscitation, ICU. Household contacts need rifampin prophylaxis.
HSP has palpable purpura on legs with abdominal pain and arthritis. Not rapid onset of shock.
ITP causes bruising and petechiae but not fever, hypotension, or toxic appearance.
KD has prolonged fever, not rapid onset with shock. Rash is polymorphous, not petechial.

rationale: Meningococcemia: give antibiotics (ceftriaxone) promptly. Do not delay LP. Chemoprophylaxis for close contacts.

question: A 41-year-old female presents with bruising and petechiae after a viral illness. Platelets 18, Hb 12, WBC 8. No splenomegaly. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: HUS: thrombocytopenia WITH microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and renal failure. This patient has normal Hb and renal function.
ITP: isolated thrombocytopenia in a well-appearing child after viral illness. Observation if no mucosal bleeding. Steroids or IVIG for significant bleeding.
Aplastic anemia: pancytopenia with low reticulocytes, not isolated thrombocytopenia.
Leukemia causes pancytopenia, not isolated thrombocytopenia. Would have anemia, neutropenia, and abnormal WBC.

rationale: ITP: observe if mild. Steroids ± IVIG for mucosal bleeding or platelet <10.

question: A 42-year-old male presents with pallor, fever, bone pain, and hepatosplenomegaly. CBC shows Hb 6, WBC 80,000 with blasts, platelets 40. Bone marrow shows >25% lymphoblasts. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Aplastic crisis causes reticulocytopenia and rapid drop in Hb but does not cause leukocytosis with blasts.
ALL is the most common childhood cancer. Presents with cytopenias (anemia, thrombocytopenia), fever, bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly. Marrow blasts confirm diagnosis.
AML is more common in adults and presents with similar findings but Auer rods and myeloid markers differentiate.
Neuroblastoma: solid tumor of sympathetic nervous system. Presents with abdominal mass or bone pain, not leukemic blasts in marrow.

rationale: ALL: chemotherapy protocols risk-stratified by age, WBC, cytogenetics. CNS prophylaxis included.

question: A 43-year-old female presents with abdominal mass and hypertension. CT shows 8 cm suprarenal mass crossing the midline. Urine catecholamines elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Neuroblastoma: adrenal or sympathetic chain tumor, common in children <5 years. Elevated urine VMA/HVA. MIBG scan for staging. Treatment: surgery, chemotherapy, or observation for low-risk.
Wilms is an intrarenal tumor presenting as an abdominal mass. It does not cross the midline. Hypertension can occur but urine catecholamines are normal.
Rhabdomyosarcoma arises from muscle tissue anywhere in the body, not specifically from adrenal with catecholamine production.
Pheochromocytoma presents with paroxysmal hypertension, palpitations, and headache. Rare in children.

rationale: Neuroblastoma: common in <5 years. MIBG scan for staging. Risk-stratified treatment: observation (low-risk) to intensive chemo (high-risk).

question: A 15-day-old full-term neonate presents with tachypnea, grunting, and nasal flaring immediately after C-section delivery. Chest X-ray shows retained fetal fluid with prominent interstitial markings. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: MAS occurs in post-term infants with meconium-stained fluid. CXR shows coarse, patchy infiltrates. This infant had C-section without meconium history.
TTN: self-limited respiratory distress after C-section due to delayed fetal lung fluid clearance. Supportive care with O2. Usually resolves in 24-48 hours.
Congenital pneumonia presents with respiratory distress and CXR infiltrates. Usually has maternal risk factors (chorioamnionitis, prolonged ROM).
RDS affects preterm infants due to surfactant deficiency. CXR shows ground-glass appearance with air bronchograms.

rationale: TTN: self-limited after C-section. Supportive care. Distinguish from pneumonia and RDS.

question: A 16-day-old neonate presents with jaundice on day 2. Total bilirubin 18 mg/dL, direct 0.5. Mother is blood type O, baby is A. Direct Coombs test positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: ABO incompatibility: mother O, baby A or B. Mild to moderate hemolysis with positive direct Coombs. Management: phototherapy. Exchange transfusion if severe.
Physiologic jaundice appears after 24 hours, peaks at day 3-5, and resolves by day 7. Bilirubin typically <15, and Coombs is negative.
Breast milk jaundice appears after day 5-7 and peaks at 2-3 weeks. Coombs is negative and onset is later.
Rh incompatibility typically causes more severe hemolysis and is prevented by RhoGAM. First pregnancy is rarely affected.

rationale: Neonatal jaundice: assess risk factors, plot on Bhutani nomogram. Phototherapy per AAP guidelines.

question: A 46-year-old male presents with polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, and DKA (pH 7.1, HCO3 8). What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: DI presents with polyuria and polydipsia but normal blood glucose. Not weight loss or DKA.
Psychogenic polydipsia: excessive water intake, normal glucose, not DKA.
T2DM: typically presents in older, overweight children with acanthosis nigricans and family history. DKA is less common.
T1DM: autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells. Presents with classic triad (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss) ± DKA. Management: insulin, fluids, K+ replacement.

rationale: T1DM: insulin therapy. DKA management: fluids, insulin infusion, K+ replacement. Monitor cerebral edema.

question: A 47-year-old female presents with short stature (height -3.5 SD), delayed bone age, and low IGF-1. Growth hormone stimulation test shows peak GH 3.5 ng/mL (normal >10). What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Cushing: growth failure WITH weight gain, central obesity, striae. This patient is not described as overweight.
Hypothyroidism: elevated TSH, low T4, delayed bone age. Always check thyroid status before GH testing.
Constitutional delay: delayed puberty, bone age matches height age, normal growth velocity. GH stimulation test is normal.
GH deficiency: short stature, delayed bone age, low IGF-1, and failed GH stimulation test. Treatment: recombinant GH therapy. Rule out other causes (hypothyroidism, chronic disease).

rationale: GH deficiency: confirm with stimulation test. Replace with daily GH injections. Monitor height velocity.

question: A 19-day-old neonate presents with poor feeding, lethargy, vomiting, and metabolic acidosis with increased anion gap, hypoglycemia, hyperammonemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Inborn error of metabolism (organic acidemia or urea cycle defect)
options.rationale: IEM should be suspected in neonates with unexplained metabolic acidosis, hyperammonemia, hypoglycemia, and neurologic deterioration. Workup: ammonia, amino acids, acylcarnitine profile, urine organic acids.
Sepsis can present similarly but would have inflammatory markers and positive cultures. IEM should be considered when sepsis is excluded or atypical.
Hyperinsulinism causes hypoglycemia with low ketones. Does not cause metabolic acidosis or hyperammonemia.
CAH presents with virilization or salt wasting (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia), not metabolic acidosis with hyperammonemia.

rationale: Suspected IEM: check glucose, ammonia, lactate, ABG, urine ketones. Consult genetics and metabolic specialist.

question: A 3-year-old female presents with bilious vomiting and a palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. Currant-jelly stools. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Appendicitis: RLQ pain, fever, not currant-jelly stools or sausage-shaped mass.
Malrotation presents with bilious vomiting in first month of life, not currant-jelly stools or sausage-shaped mass.
Intussusception: telescoping of bowel. Classic triad: colicky abdominal pain, currant-jelly stools, palpable sausage-shaped mass. Air/contrast enema is diagnostic and therapeutic.
Meckel: painless lower GI bleeding, not intussusception mass. Law of 2s: 2% of population, 2 inches long, 2 feet from ileocecal valve.

rationale: Intussusception: air enema reduces 80-95%. Surgery for failed reduction or peritonitis.

question: A 4-year-old male presents with acute right lower quadrant pain, fever, and anorexia. McDonald sign positive. WBC 15. Ultrasound shows non-compressible appendix. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: With clear signs of appendicitis (fever, RLQ tenderness, elevated WBC, positive US), surgery should not be delayed.
Acute appendicitis with peritonitis signs requires urgent appendectomy. Abscess may be managed with drainage + interval appendectomy.
Non-operative management is for uncomplicated appendicitis without peritonitis. This patient has signs of peritoneal irritation.
CT drainage is for abscess >3 cm. This patient has acute appendicitis without evidence of abscess.

rationale: Pediatric appendicitis: laparoscopic appendectomy. Antibiotics for 24 hours post-op for uncomplicated.

question: A 5-year-old female is due for routine immunizations. Up to date with all vaccines. Which vaccines are given at this age (4-6 years)?

options.rationale: 4-6 year vaccines: DTaP (5th dose), IPV (4th dose), MMR (2nd dose), varicella (2nd dose). These complete the childhood immunization series before school entry.
Multiple booster doses are scheduled at 4-6 years. At 11-12 years: Tdap, HPV, and meningococcal vaccines.
MMR and varicella boosters are also due at 4-6 years, along with DTaP and IPV.
DTaP and IPV are also required at 4-6 years to complete the primary series.

rationale: 4-6 year visit: DTaP, IPV, MMR, varicella boosters. Also screen vision, hearing, and development.

question: A 6-month-old male presents with acute watery diarrhea for 3 days, vomiting, and decreased urine output. Dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, skin tenting. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.rationale: Antidiarrheals are contraindicated in children due to risk of ileus, toxic megacolon, and side effects.
Most gastroenteritis is viral. Antibiotics are reserved for dysentery, suspected cholera, or immunocompromised patients.
Holding feeds in non-severe diarrhea prolongs illness. Early refeeding is recommended. Antibiotics are not indicated for acute watery diarrhea.

options.text: ORS or IV fluids based on dehydration severity
options.rationale: Assess dehydration first. Mild-moderate: ORS. Severe: IV bolus. Continue breastfeeding. Zinc 20 mg daily for 14 days reduces duration and severity.

rationale: Manage dehydration severity with ORS or IV. Zinc reduces duration. Continue feeding.

question: A 7-month-old female presents with fever 39.5°C and a 3-minute generalized seizure that stopped spontaneously. Now alert and playing. No prior seizures. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Simple febrile seizure: age 6m-5y, generalized, <15 min, single in 24h, no postictal deficit. No workup beyond fever source identification needed.
Meningitis should be considered if the child is ill-appearing or has nuchal rigidity. This child returned to baseline immediately.
Epilepsy requires 2+ unprovoked seizures. Febrile seizures are provoked by fever and generally do not predict epilepsy.
Complex: focal, >15 min, or multiple in 24h. This seizure is generalized, brief, and single.

rationale: Simple febrile seizure: age 6m-5y, generalized <15min. Manage fever. No EEG or imaging needed.

question: A 8-year-old male with persistent coughing fits ending with a whooping sound, post-tussive vomiting, and no fever. Not immunized. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Bronchiolitis presents with wheezing, respiratory distress, and fever in infants <12 months. Not paroxysmal cough.
Croup presents with barking cough, stridor, and hoarseness. Not paroxysmal whooping fits.
Foreign body presents with sudden onset of coughing and choking in a previously well child. Not paroxysmal with whoop.
Pertussis: paroxysmal cough with inspiratory whoop, post-tussive vomiting, afebrile. Most severe in infants. Diagnosis: PCR or culture. Treatment: macrolide antibiotic.

rationale: Pertussis: paroxysmal cough + whoop. Macrolide treatment. Prevention: DTaP vaccine.

question: A 9-year-old female presents with wheezing and respiratory distress after playing with a cat. PEFR 40% predicted. After 3 salbutamol nebulizations and oral prednisone, PEFR remains 45%. What is the next step?

options.rationale: One dose of steroids is adequate for acute exacerbation. Additional steroids take hours to work and do not provide immediate benefit.
Aminophylline is no longer recommended in pediatric acute asthma due to side effects and lack of additional benefit beyond SABA and steroids.
Intubation is reserved for impending respiratory failure (silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion). Not yet indicated.
IV MgSO4 is the next step for severe asthma not responding to SABA and steroids. It reduces hospital admission rates and improves PEFR within 30 minutes.

rationale: Severe asthma not responding to SABA+steroids: IV MgSO4. IV salbutamol for life-threatening cases.

question: A 10-month-old male presents with Hb 8.5, MCV 70, ferritin 5. Diet history: prolonged breastfeeding with no iron-rich solids. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: ACD has normal or high ferritin and low iron/TIBC. Not associated with dietary iron deficiency.
IDA: microcytic anemia with low ferritin from inadequate dietary iron. Most common in 9-24 month olds. Treatment: oral iron 3-6 mg/kg/day plus dietary modification.
Lead poisoning causes microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling. History of pica or environmental exposure would be present.
Thalassemia minor has microcytosis out of proportion to anemia, normal ferritin, and elevated HbA2 on electrophoresis.

rationale: IDA in toddlers: screen with CBC and ferritin. Treat with oral iron. Prevent with iron-fortified cereals after 6 months.

question: A 11-month-old female presents with cough, wheeze, and respiratory distress for 2 days. RSV positive. O2 88%, RR 60. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Bronchodilators are not routinely recommended in bronchiolitis. May trial but discontinue if no objective improvement.

options.text: Oxygen if SpO2 <90%, nasal suctioning, supportive care
options.rationale: Bronchiolitis is managed supportively. O2 for SpO2 <90%. Nasal suctioning before feeds. Most resolves in 7-10 days. No routine bronchodilators or steroids.
Antibiotics are for secondary bacterial infection. Most bronchiolitis is viral and antibiotics are not indicated.
Steroids do not improve outcomes in viral bronchiolitis and are not recommended unless the child has concomitant asthma.

rationale: Bronchiolitis: supportive care (O2, suctioning). No bronchodilators or steroids routinely.

question: A 12-year-old male presents with fever, cough, and tachypnea for 3 days. CXR shows right lower lobe consolidation. O2 96%, no indrawing. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Non-severe CAP: oral amoxicillin 90 mg/kg/day. Hospitalize if hypoxia, indrawing, toxic appearance, or inability to tolerate oral.
Macrolides are for atypical pneumonia (Mycoplasma) in school-age children. Amoxicillin is first-line for typical lobar pneumonia in younger children.
Consolidation on CXR with fever suggests bacterial pneumonia requiring antibiotics.
Hospitalization is for hypoxia, significant indrawing, or toxic appearance. This patient has no severity criteria.

rationale: Pediatric CAP: amoxicillin first-line. Hospitalize if hypoxia, indrawing, or toxic.

question: A 13-year-old female presents with ear pain and fever for 2 days. Otoscopy shows bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane with decreased mobility. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Augmentin is reserved for treatment failure after 48-72 hours of amoxicillin or recent antibiotic use.
Tubes are for recurrent AOM (≥3 in 6 months or ≥4 in 12 months) or chronic OME, not first episode.
Acute otitis media: antibiotics if age <2 years, bilateral, severe symptoms, or otorrhea. Amoxicillin first-line. Observation option for older children with mild symptoms.
Observation is appropriate for children ≥2 years with mild unilateral AOM. This patient has fever and ear pain suggesting moderate severity.

rationale: AOM: amoxicillin first-line. Observation for mild cases in older children. Prevention: pneumococcal and influenza vaccines.

question: A 14-year-old male presents with fever, sore throat, and exudative tonsillitis. Rapid strep test positive. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Penicillin V or amoxicillin for 10 days
options.rationale: Group A strep pharyngitis requires antibiotics to prevent rheumatic fever. Penicillin or amoxicillin for 10 days is first-line.
Macrolides are alternatives for penicillin-allergic patients but are not first-line due to resistance concerns.
Steroids are not indicated for uncomplicated GAS pharyngitis. Antibiotics alone are sufficient.
Rapid strep test positive confirms GAS infection. Antibiotics are indicated to prevent suppurative and non-suppurative complications.

rationale: GAS pharyngitis: penicillin 10 days prevents rheumatic fever. Treat even if mild.

question: A 15-month-old female presents with fever for 3 days without source. Urine dipstick shows leukocyte esterase positive and nitrite positive. Urine culture grows E. coli >10^5 CFU/mL. What is the appropriate imaging after first febrile UTI?

options.rationale: VCUG is indicated after abnormal US, recurrent UTIs, or atypical/complicated UTI. Not for all first UTIs.
First febrile UTI in child <2 years: renal/bladder US to assess for anatomic abnormalities. VCUG if US abnormal or recurrent UTI.
DMSA evaluates renal scarring after pyelonephritis. Not routine after first UTI.
Children <2 years with first febrile UTI require renal/bladder US per guidelines.

rationale: First febrile UTI in <2 years: renal US. VCUG if abnormal US or recurrent.

question: A 16-year-old male presents with chronic diarrhea, bloating, and poor weight gain. Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA strongly positive. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: PPIs do not treat celiac disease. They might mask symptoms without addressing the underlying autoimmune response.
Secondary lactose intolerance may coexist but gluten avoidance is the primary treatment for celiac disease.
Budesonide is for refractory celiac disease. First-line is dietary gluten elimination.
Celiac disease requires strict lifelong gluten-free diet. Symptoms improve within weeks. Serology normalizes over months. Monitor for nutritional deficiencies.

rationale: Celiac disease: gluten-free diet. Monitor growth, serology, and nutritional status.

question: A 17-year-old female presents with palpable purpura on the legs and buttocks, abdominal pain, and arthritis. Recent URTI. Platelets normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Meningococcemia presents with fever, petechial/purpuric rash, and ill appearance. This child has abdominal pain and arthritis without toxic appearance.
ITP presents with petechiae and bruising with LOW platelets. This patient has normal platelets.
Kawasaki has fever >5 days, conjunctivitis, oral changes, and extremity changes. Not palpable purpura on lower extremities.
HSP: palpable purpura + abdominal pain + arthritis. Normal platelets. Usually self-limited. Steroids for severe abdominal pain or renal involvement. Monitor urine for nephritis.

rationale: HSP: palpable purpura + arthritis + abdominal pain. Self-limited. Steroids for severe GI or renal involvement.

question: A 18-month-old male presents with bowed legs and widened wrists. Not yet walking. Formula-fed, limited sun exposure. Alkaline phosphatase elevated, calcium low-normal, phosphorus low. X-ray shows cupping and fraying of metaphyses. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Renal osteodystrophy occurs in CKD with elevated creatinine and abnormal calcium/phosphate. This patient has no renal history.
Hypophosphatasia has low ALP (not elevated), along with bone deformities and fractures.
Rickets: bowed legs, widened wrists, hypocalcemia, low phosphorus, elevated ALP. X-ray: metaphyseal cupping and fraying. Treatment: vitamin D and calcium supplementation.
Blount disease is a growth disorder of the proximal tibia causing bowing. X-ray shows tibial vara without metaphyseal changes of rickets.

rationale: Rickets: vitamin D + calcium supplementation. Prevent with vitamin D 400 IU/day from birth.

question: A 19-year-old female presents with constipation since infancy, ribbon-like stools, and failure to thrive. Rectal exam shows empty rectum with tight anal canal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Congenital hypothyroidism presents with poor feeding, hypotonia, and prolonged jaundice. Constipation may occur but not ribbon-like stools.
Celiac presents with diarrhea, bloating, and malabsorption, not constipation from birth.
Functional constipation develops after infancy with stool-withholding behavior, palpable fecal mass, and normal rectal tone.
Hirschsprung: constipation from birth, ribbon stools, empty rectum on exam. Diagnosis: barium enema shows transition zone. Treatment: surgical resection of aganglionic segment.

rationale: Hirschsprung: constipation from birth, empty rectum. Barium enema + rectal biopsy for diagnosis. Surgical resection.

question: A 20-month-old male presents with recurrent infections including pneumonia, oral thrush, and failure to thrive. Low immunoglobulins, absent B cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Hyper-IgM: normal/high IgM with low IgG/IgA/IgE, opportunistic infections (PCP, Cryptosporidium).
Bruton disease: recurrent infections starting after 6 months (maternal IgG wanes), low immunoglobulins, absent B cells. Treatment: IVIG replacement.
SCID presents earlier (first months) with severe infections, lymphopenia, and failure to thrive. T cells are affected.
Wiskott-Aldrich: eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets, recurrent infections, and autoimmune disease.

rationale: Bruton agammaglobulinemia: recurrent infections after 6 months, low immunoglobulins, absent B cells. IVIG therapy.

question: A 21-year-old female presents with ascending weakness starting in the legs over 3 days, areflexia, and no sensory level. Lumbar puncture shows elevated protein with normal WBC. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Myasthenia gravis has fluctuating weakness, ptosis, diplopia, and fatiguability. Not ascending paralysis.
GBS: ascending paralysis, areflexia, albuminocytologic dissociation (high protein, normal cells). Often post-infectious. Treatment: IVIG or plasmapheresis.
Transverse myelitis has a sensory level and acute onset of paraplegia with spinal cord inflammation on MRI.
Polio presents with asymmetric flaccid paralysis with fever. Nearly eradicated due to vaccination.

rationale: GBS: ascending paralysis, areflexia, high CSF protein. IVIG or plasmapheresis. Respiratory monitoring essential.

question: A 22-year-old male presents with a first-time afebrile generalized seizure. EEG shows generalized spike-wave discharges. Neurologic exam normal. MRI normal. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are for acute active seizures or status epilepticus. This patient has already stopped seizing.

options.text: Start antiepileptic drug (valproic acid or levetiracetam)
options.rationale: First unprovoked seizure with epileptiform EEG has ~50% recurrence risk. AED therapy reduces recurrence. Valproate or levetiracetam are first-line for generalized epilepsy.
With abnormal EEG, recurrence risk is high and treatment is recommended. Observation may be appropriate if EEG is normal.
Carbamazepine is first-line for focal seizures, not generalized spike-wave epilepsy. Valproate or levetiracetam are preferred.

rationale: First unprovoked seizure with abnormal EEG: start AED. Valproate for generalized, carbamazepine for focal.

question: A 23-year-old female with cerebral palsy (GMFCS III) presents with worsening hip pain and difficulty sitting. X-ray shows >50% femoral head subluxation. What is the most appropriate management?

options.rationale: Botox reduces spasticity and may slow subluxation progression but does not correct established subluxation >50%.
PT maintains range of motion but cannot reverse structural subluxation. Surgical intervention is needed.

options.text: Referral to orthopedics for surgical reconstruction
options.rationale: Hip subluxation >50% in CP requires surgical reconstruction (femoral osteotomy ± pelvic osteotomy) to prevent dislocation, pain, and loss of function.
Casting is for developmental dysplasia in infants, not for spastic hip subluxation in CP.

rationale: CP hip surveillance: X-ray every 6-12 months. Surgical reconstruction for subluxation >50% or dislocation.

question: A 24-year-old male presents with episodic unilateral pounding headache with nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia. Relieved by sleep. Neuro exam normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Pseudotumor: headache with papilledema, visual disturbances, elevated CSF pressure. Neuroimaging is normal.
Tension headache: bilateral band-like pressure, no nausea or photophobia. Less disabling than migraine.
Migraine: episodic unilateral pulsating headache, nausea, photophobia/phonophobia, relieved by sleep. Treatment: ibuprofen or sumatriptan. Prevention for frequent attacks.
Cluster: unilateral severe pain around eye with autonomic features (lacrimation, rhinorrhea). Duration 15-180 minutes.

rationale: Pediatric migraine: acute treatment (NSAIDs, triptans). Prevention (amitriptyline, topiramate) for frequent attacks.

question: A 14-day-old female presents with cyanosis and respiratory distress. Pulse oximetry: preductal 95%, postductal 75%. Chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly with pulmonary edema. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: TAPVR presents with cyanosis and pulmonary edema. Not differential cyanosis.
TOF presents with cyanosis and hypercyanotic spells, not differential cyanosis. Echocardiogram shows VSD, overriding aorta, RV hypertrophy, pulmonary stenosis.
Differential cyanosis (higher preductal O2) suggests coarctation. Ductus supplies descending aorta. Start PGE1 to maintain ductal patency. Surgical repair after stabilization.
TGA presents with severe cyanosis in first day, equal pre and postductal saturations. Requires balloon atrial septostomy.

rationale: Duct-dependent coarctation: start PGE1, ICU, surgical repair. Differential cyanosis is the key sign.

question: A 26-year-old male presents with fever and joint pain 3 weeks after strep throat. Cardiac exam shows a new murmur. ECG shows prolonged PR interval. ESR elevated, ASO titer elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Kawasaki: fever >5 days, conjunctivitis, oral changes, rash, extremity changes. Not associated with preceding strep throat.
Rheumatic fever: Jones criteria require 2 major (carditis, arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules) or 1 major + 2 minor. Treatment: aspirin, penicillin prophylaxis.
Endocarditis presents with fever, murmur, and positive blood cultures. Not preceded by strep throat with ASO elevation.
JIA presents with prolonged fever and arthritis but not carditis or ASO elevation.

rationale: Rheumatic fever: follows GAS pharyngitis. Jones criteria. Penicillin prophylaxis prevents recurrence and rheumatic heart disease.

question: A 27-month-old female presents with poor feeding, tachypnea, and failure to thrive. Loud holosystolic murmur at left lower sternal border. Chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascularity. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: ASD has wide fixed splitting of S2 with systolic murmur at left upper sternal border. Often asymptomatic in infancy.

Large VSD presents at 4-8 weeks (when pulmonary resistance drops) with heart failure, holosystolic murmur at LLSB, and increased pulmonary vascularity. Treatment: surgical closure if failure to thrive.
PDA has continuous machinery murmur at left infraclavicular area. Bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure.
TOF presents with cyanosis and right-sided aortic arch. Murmur is systolic at left upper sternal border from pulmonary stenosis.

rationale: Large VSD: heart failure at 4-8 weeks. Medical management first, surgical closure if failure.

question: A 28-month-old male presents with barking cough, stridor, and hoarseness for 2 days, worse at night. Mild chest wall indrawing. O2 95%. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Epiglottitis: acute onset, high fever, drooling, tripod positioning. Now rare due to Hib vaccine.
Bacterial tracheitis presents with high fever, toxic appearance, and thick purulent secretions. Requires intubation and antibiotics.
Croup: barking cough, stridor, hoarseness. Viral (parainfluenza). Management: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg. Nebulized epinephrine for moderate-severe stridor at rest.
Foreign body: sudden onset of choking and cough in a previously well child. Not barking cough worse at night.

rationale: Croup: dexamethasone first-line. Nebulized epinephrine for moderate-severe distress.

question: A 29-year-old female presents with recurrent sinopulmonary infections, pancreatic insufficiency, and failure to thrive. Sweat chloride 85 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: PCD presents with chronic respiratory infections and situs inversus in 50%. Sweat chloride is normal.
SCID presents with severe infections from infancy, not chronic sinopulmonary disease with pancreatic insufficiency.

CF: autosomal recessive, defective CFTR gene. Sweat chloride >60 confirms diagnosis. Multisystem: sinopulmonary, pancreatic, hepatobiliary, and male infertility. Treatment: airway clearance, enzymes, antibiotics.
Asthma presents with wheezing, not pancreatic insufficiency or failure to thrive. Sweat chloride is normal.

rationale: CF: sweat chloride >60 confirms diagnosis. CFTR modulators (ivacaftor) for specific mutations.

question: A 30-year-old male presents with chronic wet cough, purulent sputum, and digital clubbing. CT chest shows cylindrical bronchiectasis in the right middle lobe. What is the most common underlying cause?

options.rationale: ABPA presents in asthmatics or CF patients with pulmonary infiltrates and elevated IgE. Not typical isolated lobar bronchiectasis.
Alpha-1 causes panacinar emphysema and liver disease, not bronchiectasis.
